2. The call stack is where currently running functions live. When your code calls a function, that function is pushed onto the stack. When it returns, it is popped off. As long as the stack is busy, no other queued JavaScript callback can begin running.

3. The runtime environment, such as a browser or Node.js, provides APIs like timers, network handling, DOM events, file I/O, and message channels. Those host features do work outside the main JavaScript call stack and later schedule callbacks for JavaScript to run.

4. A useful mental model is: synchronous code runs first, completely, before queued asynchronous callbacks get a chance. If your script contains ten lines of direct code and one `setTimeout`, the direct code will finish before the timer callback can run, even if the timer delay is zero.

5. The event loop repeatedly checks whether the current stack is empty. When it is empty, the runtime can take pending work from its queues and move the next callback onto the stack. That is the “loop” part: check, dequeue work, run it, repeat.

6. There are different categories of queued work, and one of the most important distinctions is between microtasks and macrotasks. Promise reactions such as `.then`, `catch`, `finally`, and `queueMicrotask` go into the microtask queue, while timers, many I/O callbacks, and UI events are macrotask-style work in simplified explanations.

2. The call stack is where currently running functions live. When your code calls a function, that function is pushed onto the stack. When it returns, it is popped off. As long as the stack is busy, no other queued JavaScript callback can begin running.

3. The runtime environment, such as a browser or Node.js, provides APIs like timers, network handling, DOM events, file I/O, and message channels. Those host features do work outside the main JavaScript call stack and later schedule callbacks for JavaScript to run.

4. A useful mental model is: synchronous code runs first, completely, before queued asynchronous callbacks get a chance. If your script contains ten lines of direct code and one `setTimeout`, the direct code will finish before the timer callback can run, even if the timer delay is zero.

5. The event loop repeatedly checks whether the current stack is empty. When it is empty, the runtime can take pending work from its queues and move the next callback onto the stack. That is the “loop” part: check, dequeue work, run it, repeat.
